S.gx_title: The Analects relationship map: how the 498 chapters connect | Yikonglu
S.gx_desc: Same question, different answers; lines that appear twice; the chapters where each of the 197 people appears.
S.gx_lead: The Analects has 20 books and 498 chapters. They look like scattered sayings, but they are connected throughout. The same line appears in two places, Confucius answers the same question differently for different people, and one disciple turns up in dozens of chapters. There are {n} links in all.
S.gx_all_note: Each dot on the circle is a chapter, with the 20 books in order around the ring. Dark dots are chapters already taught. Green lines join a line that appears twice in the book ({hj} pairs). Ochre lines join the answers to the same question ({wd} groups). Tap a chapter to see what it connects to.
S.gx_all_aria: Relationship map of the 498 chapters of the Analects
S.gx_pick: Tap any chapter on the circle.
S.gx_nolink: This chapter has no lines on the map. Its chapter page lists people, other books and more under “Connections”.
S.gx_wd_note: The same question, answered differently for different people. This is the most important thread in the Analects: the answer follows the person.
S.gx_rw_note: The Analects names {n} people. Tap one: the inner ring shows the chapters they appear in, and the outer ring shows the people who most often appear in the same chapters, with the number of chapters they share.
S.gx_q_ph: Search a name, e.g. Zilu, Yan Hui, Guan Zhong

items.a: The humane put the hard work first and the reward after.
To overcome the self and return to ritual is humaneness.
What you do not want for yourself, do not impose on others.
The humane are slow to speak.
Love people.
Be respectful at home, reverent in your duties, and loyal to others.
Serve the worthiest of its high officers; befriend the most humane of its scholars.
items.note: He asked how to practice humaneness (為仁).

items.a: Respectfulness, generosity, trustworthiness, diligence, kindness.
Do not go against it.
Let your parents' only worry be that you might fall ill.
Without reverence, what is the difference?
The countenance is the hard part.
Enough food, enough arms, and the trust of the people.
Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son.
Keep it in mind without weariness; carry it out with loyalty.
To govern is to set right.
You govern; what need is there for killing?
Go before them; toil for them.
Put your officers to work first, pardon small faults, promote the worthy and able.
Those near are pleased, and those far away come.
Do not seek speed; do not look to small gains.
Honor the five excellences; banish the four evils.
items.note: He asked how to take part in government.

items.a: He acts first, and his words follow.
The gentleman is free from anxiety and fear.
He cultivates himself with reverence.
Plain and upright and loving what is right, attentive to words and observant of faces, mindful to put himself below others.
items.note: He asked what makes a scholar “accomplished” (達).

items.a: He conducts himself with a sense of shame, and when sent on missions abroad he does not disgrace his ruler's commission.
Earnest, encouraging, and genial.
Devote yourself to what is right for the people; revere the spirits but keep them at a distance.
Know people.
Hold to loyalty and trustworthiness, and move toward what is right.
Put the work first and the reward after.

4.note: Book of Songs, Wei Feng, Qi Yu: “As if cut, as if filed; as if carved, as if polished.” (如切如磋，如琢如磨。)

7.note: Book of Songs, Lu Song, Jiong: “Thoughts without swerving; so the horses go forth.” (思無邪，思馬斯徂。)

8.note: Mencius, Teng Wen Gong I, chapter 2: Zengzi said, “In life, serve them according to ritual; in death, bury them according to ritual and sacrifice to them according to ritual…”

10.note: Book of Songs, Wei Feng, Shuo Ren: “Her artful smile so lovely, her fine eyes so clear.” (巧笑倩兮，美目盼兮。)

12.note: Mencius, Gongsun Chou I, chapter 7: Confucius said, “Humaneness is what makes a neighborhood beautiful.” (孔子曰：里仁為美。)

13.note: Mencius, Gongsun Chou I, chapter 7: “If one chooses not to dwell in humaneness, how can one be wise?” (擇不處仁，焉得智？)

23.note: Book of Songs, Xiao Ya, Xiao Min: “In fear and trembling, as if at the edge of a deep abyss, as if treading on thin ice.” (戰戰兢兢，如臨深淵，如履薄冰。)

25.note: Mencius, Teng Wen Gong I, chapter 4: Confucius said, “Great indeed was Yao as a ruler!” (孔子曰：大哉，堯之為君！)

26.note: Mencius, Teng Wen Gong I, chapter 4: “Only Heaven is great, and only Yao modeled himself on it.” (惟天為大，惟堯則之。)

27.note: Mencius, Teng Wen Gong I, chapter 4: “So vast! The people could find no name for it!” (蕩蕩乎，民無能名焉！)

31.note: Book of Songs, Bei Feng, Xiong Zhi: “Neither envious nor grasping: how could he not be good?” (不忮不求，何用不臧。)

37.note: Book of Songs, Xiao Ya, Wo Xing Qi Ye: “Truly it is not for wealth, but only for novelty.” (成不以富，亦祇以異。)

45.note: Book of Songs, Bei Feng, Pao You Ku Ye: “Where it is deep, wade through in your clothes; where it is shallow, lift your hem.” (深則厲，淺則揭。)

57.note: The two lines “By nature people are close; by practice they grow far apart” (性相近，习相远) come straight from Confucius's own words.

58.note: Mencius's mother moved house three times to find the right neighbors. Commentators all explain the story with this chapter: choose a place to live where humaneness prevails.

59.note: “What will one do when old?” (老何为): if one does not study when young and has made no progress by forty or fifty, one is not worth being in awe of.

60.note: The Beiyao commentary closes its exhortation to study with Yang Huo's words urging Confucius to take office: time does not wait for us.

61.note: “Jade uncut does not become a vessel” (玉不琢，不成器): Zigong uses the Songs to say a person must be shaped the way jade is worked, by cutting, filing, carving and polishing.

62.note: Artisans complete their work in their workshops, and the gentleman reaches the Way through learning. This follows directly on “If people do not learn, they do not know what is right” (人不学，不知义).

63.note: “Keep close to teachers and friends” (亲师友): which friends? Three kinds: the upright, the trustworthy, and the well-informed.

64.note: “Filial and fraternal duty first, knowledge second” (首孝悌，次见闻): Wang Xiang and Atsumi both cite this chapter to support that order.

65.note: How to use “knowledge” (见闻): listen much, look much, and set aside whatever you are unsure of.

66.note: Kong Rong giving up the pears teaches a younger brother's duty. Youzi says filial and fraternal duty is the root of humaneness.

67.note: The Three Bonds set out the roles of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife. In Confucius's version, each first fulfills his own part.

68.note: “These four seasons revolve without end” (此四时，运不穷): Heaven does not speak, yet the seasons still run their course.

69.note: “In accord with the center” (应乎中): the Pole Star stays in the center without moving, and all the stars turn around it.

70.note: The Yinshu commentary explains the “Five Constants” with Huang Kan's subcommentary on this chapter: the Three Bonds and Five Constants do not change for a hundred generations.

71.note: Trustworthiness (信) is the last of the Five Constants: if a person cannot be trusted, I do not know what he can do.

72.note: The passage on the six grains goes well with this line from the old man with the basket: one whose limbs do not toil cannot even tell the five grains apart.

73.note: However important the six domestic animals are, they count for less than people. When the stable burned, Confucius asked only whether anyone was hurt.

74.note: The seven emotions need not be extinguished, only kept in measure: joy without excess, grief that does no harm.

75.note: The eight sounds are musical instruments. Confucius speaks of what music is for: a person's character is finally completed in music.

76.note: Music is more than bells and drums. Read this alongside the “eight sounds” (八音).

77.note: “The ruler respectful, the minister loyal” (君则敬，臣则忠): the ruler treats his ministers with ritual, and the minister serves his ruler with loyalty. Each side has its own duty.

78.note: The spirit of the Ten Duties: each role fulfills its own part.

79.note: “When the Elementary Learning is done, go on to the Four Books” (小学终，至四书): first learn how to be a person, then study texts with the energy left over.

80.note: Begin with sweeping, answering and replying, and rise step by step. That is the path from the Elementary Learning to the Four Books.

81.note: “The Analects has twenty books” (论语者，二十篇): click through for the contents of all twenty books.

82.note: The first chapter shows what “recording good words” (记善言) looks like: one saying, one principle.

83.note: Confucius had already called the two characters in the title Zhongyong (中庸, the Mean) the highest virtue.

84.note: Read the passage on the three Changes alongside Confucius saying he would study the Changes in his later years.

85.note: This one line of Confucius covers the order of the Songs, Rites and Music among the Six Classics.

86.note: “Our Duke of Zhou made the Rites of Zhou” (我周公，作周礼): Confucius says the Zhou rites drew on the Xia and Shang, so he follows Zhou.

87.note: “Rites and music complete” (礼乐备): Confucius told his son that without learning ritual he would have nothing to stand on.

88.note: The “transmit” (述) in “transmitting the sages' words” (述圣言) is the same 述 as in Confucius's “I transmit and do not create.”

89.note: On why one “should recite and chant” (当讽咏) the Songs, the Beiyao commentary cites this very chapter.

90.note: Wenzhongzi Wang Tong's Zhongshuo was modeled on the Analects, and commentators all compare the two.

91.note: Wang Xiang explains Yao with this very line in which Confucius praises Yao.

92.note: “Tang and You Yu” (唐有虞) refers to Yao and Shun. Shun governed the world with five worthy ministers.

93.note: King Wu of Zhou's “ten ministers of 乱”: here 乱 means to govern, so these are ten ministers able to set disorder right.

94.note: The Three Kings of Xia, Shang and Zhou followed one another, and their rites were added to and cut back in ways that can be known.

95.note: What it looks like when “the royal order fell” (王纲坠): rites, music and military campaigns no longer come from the Son of Heaven.

96.note: “The Five Hegemons grew strong” (五霸强): Confucius both praises and criticizes two of the hegemons.

97.note: The hegemons had their merits too: Confucius credits Guan Zhong with setting the whole world in order.

98.note: The word “usurped” (篡) in “Wang Mang usurped” (王莽篡) is the label historians fixed on him. Once the name is settled, right and wrong are clear.

99.note: Before he usurped the throne, Wang Mang was humble and courteous. Judge people over a long time, not by a single moment.

100.note: Historians argued over which of the Three Kingdoms was legitimate, and what they were arguing about was names and roles.

101.note: The Sui “passed the throne on no further and lost the line” (不再传，失统绪). Confucius had said long before that a realm gained by improper means lasts only a few generations.

102.note: The text says “received the abdication of Zhou” (受周禅), while commentators write “usurped” (篡): the dispute is between name and reality.

103.note: Most rulers of the Five Dynasties were generals who seized the throne, and their dynasties often fell within one or two reigns.

104.note: The Liao and Jin rulers who proclaimed themselves emperors can be read against this line of Confucius: whether a state truly has a ruler depends on whether it has ritual.

105.note: “Powerful eunuchs ran rampant” (权阉肆): Confucius says governing requires keeping glib flatterers at a distance.

106.note: Disaster often starts close at hand. The Ming fell to its eunuchs, trouble from right “within the screen wall.”

107.note: “Recite with the mouth, ponder with the mind” (口而诵，心而惟): reciting is learning and pondering is thinking. Neither can be left out.

108.note: “At it in the morning, at it in the evening” (朝于斯，夕于斯): Wang Xiang says this is practicing it constantly.

109.note: “It records order and chaos, so one knows rise and fall” (载治乱，知兴衰): reading history lets you infer later ages, and Confucius says a hundred generations can be known.

110.note: Confucius took Xiang Tuo as his teacher. He had no fixed teacher and learned from whoever had the Way.

111.note: The “Lu Analects” that Zhao Pu read is the same twenty-book Analects we have today.

112.note: “Already in office, he studied all the harder” (彼既仕，学且勤): whatever energy is left over from office should still go to study.

113.note: Tying one's hair to a beam and jabbing one's thigh with an awl are stories of hard study. Confucius said that when he was learning, he forgot to eat.

114.note: Grinding away is not the same as knowing how to learn: learning without thinking still leaves you confused.

115.note: On the “lofty” (卓) in “still toiling for the lofty” (犹苦卓): Yan Yuan says Confucius's learning stands lofty before him, and however hard he follows he cannot reach it.

116.note: Su Xun “first resolved to strive” (始发愤) at twenty-seven, and the Yinshu commentary cites this line of Confucius to explain 发愤.

117.note: Confucius set his heart on learning at fifteen, while Su Xun only resolved to strive at twenty-seven. Read the two side by side.

118.note: Child prodigies were ones “people called marvels” (人称奇). Confucius says the young deserve awe, but he also warns that anyone still unknown at forty or fifty does not.

119.note: After the child prodigies, the Beiyao commentary closes with “learning what is below and reaching what is above”: beyond cleverness, one must learn step by step.

120.note: “One should take warning oneself” (当自警): the warning is for yourself, not something to use against others.

121.note: Cai Wenji and Xie Daoyun were able to learn, and teaching has never made distinctions of background.

122.note: Liu Yan held office at seven, while Confucius only set his heart on learning at fifteen. Early or late does not matter. What matters is resolve.

123.note: Liu Yan's answer about the character 朋 mocked factions. Read it with Confucius's “sociable but not partisan.”

124.note: “A person who does not learn is worse than a creature” (人不学，不如物): the expanded commentary (增注) uses this line of Confucius.

125.note: “Learn when young, act when grown” (幼而学，壮而行): learning and doing take turns for a whole lifetime.

126.note: “Make your name known” (扬名声): the gentleman fears reaching the end of his life with nothing worth praising.

127.note: On the “benefit” (益) in “play brings no benefit” (戏无益), the Yinshu commentary cites this chapter: real progress takes slow work and cannot be rushed.

128.note: “Play brings no benefit” does not mean no play at all. Confucius too says “take your ease in the arts.”

129.note: Laozi says the Way cannot be put into words. Confucius likewise says Heaven never speaks, yet the four seasons still run their course.

130.note: “Achieving without dwelling on it” (功成而弗居): Shun and Yu possessed the world but did not treat it as their own.

131.note: Lü Huiqing, explaining “Do not display what is desirable, so the people's hearts are not disturbed,” cites Confucius's answer to Ji Kangzi: if you yourself were not covetous…

132.note: Heshang Gong cites this line to explain “not exalting the worthy,” writing 远美人 (“keep beautiful people at a distance”) for 远佞人 (“keep flatterers at a distance”). One character makes the difference.

133.note: Confucius calls for “promoting the worthy and able,” and Laozi says “do not exalt the worthy.” On employing people, the two schools are exact opposites.

134.note: Laozi speaks of “softening the glare and mingling with the dust” (和其光，同其尘), and Confucius of “harmonious but not the same” (和而不同). Both speak of harmony, but one merges with others while the other keeps itself.

135.note: Du Daojian notes that Laozi often says “what the ancients called” or “the established sayings have it.” He is retelling the ancients, just like Confucius's “I transmit and do not create.”

136.note: “He puts himself last, and finds himself first” (后其身而身先): think of others first and you end up standing firm yourself. Confucius too says “wishing to stand, he helps others stand.”

137.note: Laozi says “the highest good is like water,” and Confucius says “the wise delight in water.” Confucians and Daoists both compare people to water.

138.note: Looking at the same water, Confucius saw time that never stops.

139.note: “Rich and noble yet arrogant, one brings blame on oneself” (富贵而骄，自遗其咎). Confucius also says “rich without arrogance” is not enough: one should be “rich and love ritual.”

140.note: “Better to stop than to fill it to the brim” (持而盈之，不如其已) is about knowing when to stop. Confucius gives warnings for three stages: youth, prime, and old age.

141.note: “Clear and reaching in all four directions, can you be without knowing?” (明白四达，能无知乎). Confucius too says he is “without knowledge,” and when someone asks him, he probes the question from both ends.

142.note: Heshang Gong reads “the gate of Heaven” (天门) as the north pole. Confucius compares governing by virtue to the Pole Star.

143.note: Laozi says a vessel is useful because of its “emptiness” (无). Confucius says the gentleman must not be a mere vessel.

144.note: Wu Cheng cites Dong Sijing: Confucius's “four do-nots” begin with looking, which matches Laozi's “the five colors blind the eye” and “for the belly, not for the eye.”

145.note: Wang Pang, explaining “I have great trouble because I have a body,” cites Confucius's “no ego” (毋我) and says the principle is the same.

146.note: “Favor and disgrace alike are alarming” (宠辱若惊): before getting something you fear not getting it, and once you have it you fear losing it. This is just Confucius's “base fellow” (鄙夫).

147.note: “Valuing one's own person as one values the world” (贵以身为天下): commentators adapt Confucius's praise of Shun and Yu, who “possessed the world yet did not take it as their own.”

148.note: “Hold to the Way of old to manage what exists now” (执古之道，以御今之有): Confucius too says he is “faithful to antiquity and loves it.”

149.note: Only by knowing the principles of old can you handle what is in front of you. Confucius calls it “reviewing the old to understand the new” (温故而知新).

150.note: “Hesitant, as if crossing a river in winter” (豫兮若冬涉川): as careful as someone crossing an icy river in winter, just like Zengzi when he quoted the Songs.

151.note: “Solemn, like a guest” (俨兮其若客): grave and dignified like a guest. Confucius says that when you go out, act as if you were meeting an honored guest.

152.note: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, explaining “not knowing the constant, one acts rashly, and misfortune follows” (不知常，妄作，凶), cites this line: a person without constancy will meet with disgrace.

153.note: Laozi says that with the best ruler, the people merely know he exists. Confucius too praises Shun for “governing without acting” (无为而治).

154.note: “When trust is lacking, there is distrust” (信不足焉，有不信焉): Confucius too puts trust ahead of food and arms.

155.note: The ruler stays still and everyone naturally turns around him. This is exactly what Laozi calls “the very highest” (太上).

156.note: Laozi says filial piety and kindness only show up when the six relations are out of harmony. Confucius says that when those above are filial and kind, those below will be loyal. The same words, read two ways.

157.note: Confucians make filial piety the root of humaneness, but Laozi says “When the great Way is abandoned, there are humaneness and righteousness.”

158.note: Laozi wants to “abandon cleverness and discard profit,” and Confucius likewise detests “clever words and an ingratiating face.”

159.note: “Between 唯 and 阿, how great is the difference?” (唯之与阿，相去几何): 唯 is the respectful reply of a disciple to his teacher, and it is the word Zengzi used to answer Confucius.

160.note: “What others fear, one cannot fail to fear” (人之所畏，不可不畏): Confucius speaks of three things the gentleman holds in awe.

161.note: Laozi says “cut off learning and you will have no worries” (绝学无忧). Confucius says a whole day spent thinking is not as good as learning.

162.note: Chunfu's commentary, recorded by Jiao Hong, cites Su Shi's “what passes is like this, yet it has never gone,” using Confucius's sigh by the river to explain “from ancient times to now…”

163.note: Heshang Gong reads “return it whole” (全而归之) as returning one's body intact to one's parents. This is exactly what Zengzi did on his deathbed: “Uncover my feet, uncover my hands.”

164.note: “Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him” (夫唯不争，故天下莫能与之争). Confucius too says the gentleman has nothing to contend over.

165.note: Su Zhe, explaining “one who is at one with loss, loss too is glad to have” (同于失者，失亦乐得之), cites Confucius: one who sets his heart on humaneness will do no evil, and how much more one who sets it on the Way.

166.note: Laozi says a whirlwind does not last the whole morning, while Confucius likens the gentleman's virtue to the wind. The same word, wind, used two ways.

167.note: “One who boasts has no merit” (自伐者无功): Yan Yuan's wish was precisely never to boast of his own good qualities.

168.note: Meng Zhifan guarded the rear in a retreat, and on entering the city said his horse would not go faster, refusing to take credit.

169.note: Jiao Hong records Li Yue's reading 法地地，法天天，法道道 and cites as evidence the pattern of Confucius's 君君臣臣父父子子 (“let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son”).

170.note: Laozi says “Heaven is great, Earth is great, and the king too is great.” Confucius praises Yao: “Only Heaven is great, and only Yao modeled himself on it.”

171.note: The excavated texts read “the gentleman travels all day without leaving his baggage wagons” (君子终日行不离其辎重). Confucius says “a gentleman without gravity has no dignity” (君子不重则不威).

172.note: Su Zhe, explaining “good speech leaves no flaw to fault,” speaks of “speaking only when the time is right,” a phrase that comes from this chapter.

173.note: “The good person is the teacher of the one who is not good; the one who is not good is the material of the good person.” Confucius says that both the good and the bad can be our teachers.

174.note: “Always good at saving people, so no one is cast aside” (常善救人，故无弃人): Confucius too says teaching makes no distinction of background.

175.note: Jiao Hong records Lü Huiqing citing “How lofty were Shun and Yu, possessing the world yet not taking it as their own!” to explain “The world is a sacred vessel; it cannot be acted upon.”

176.note: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's commentary uses “the succession ordained by Heaven rests on your person” (历数在躬), from Yao's words when handing the throne to Shun.

177.note: “Achieve the result without pride, achieve it without boasting” (果而勿矜，果而勿伐). The commander Confucius wanted was likewise one who “approaches a task with caution and succeeds through careful planning.”

178.note: Laozi says “do not use arms to dominate the world,” and Confucius says the people must be taught for seven years before they go to war. Neither takes up arms lightly.

179.note: “Weapons are instruments of ill omen” (兵者不祥之器): war is one of the three things Confucius treated with the greatest care.

180.note: Duke Ling of Wei asked about battle formations. Confucius said he had never studied them, and left the next day.

181.note: “Once regulation begins there are names; once there are names, one should know when to stop” (始制有名，名亦既有，夫亦将知止). Confucius wants names rectified, and Laozi says that once names are established, one must know when to stop.

182.note: Su Zhe explains “one who conquers himself is strong” as “able to overcome the self and restore one's nature” (克己复性), clearly adapting Confucius's “overcome the self and return to ritual” (克己复礼).

183.note: Su Zhe explains “The great Way floods everywhere; it can go left or right” with Confucius's words about himself: “nothing I must do, nothing I must not do” (无可无不可).

184.note: "Achievement accomplished without claiming the name" (功成不名有): Confucius praises Yao, and the people could not say what was good about him.

185.note: "The Dao, when spoken, is bland and tasteless" (道之出口，淡乎其无味): pleasant words do not hold people for long.

186.note: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang defends "What is to be shrunk must first be stretched" (将欲歙之，必固张之) by citing Confucius: "One may stand firm with someone, yet not be able to weigh circumstances with him." This, he says, is expedience…

187.note: Laozi says "The Dao constantly does nothing, yet nothing is left undone" (道常无为而无不为). Confucius likewise says Shun "simply made himself reverent and faced south, nothing more."

188.note: The excavated manuscripts read "Heaven and earth will right themselves" (天地将自正). Confucius says, "If you lead with rectitude, who will dare not be upright?"

189.note: Su Zhe explains "Superior virtue is not virtuous" (上德不德) by citing Confucius at seventy: "I followed what my heart desired without overstepping the bounds."

190.note: Emperor Xuanzong explains "Ritual is the thinning of loyalty and trust" (礼者忠信之薄) by citing Confucius: is ritual merely jade and silk?

191.note: Jiao Hong records Xizhai's commentary, which uses Confucius's "My Way has one thread running through it" to explain "Those of old who attained the One" (昔之得一者).

192.note: "Reversal is the movement of the Dao" (反者道之动): Confucius too knew that, beyond holding to the constant, one must adapt to change.

193.note: Su Zhe explains "When the superior scholar hears the Dao, he practices it diligently" (上士闻道，勤而行之) and says Yan Hui was just such a superior scholar.

194.note: Jiao Hong records Lü Huiqing's commentary. Lü cites "Hear the Way in the morning, and one may die in the evening content" and says the superior scholar is one who has truly understood the Dao.

195.note: Wang Pang explains "The great vessel is completed late" (大器晚成) by citing Confucius's remark that Guan Zhong was a small vessel.

196.note: "The violent and strong do not die a natural death" (强梁者不得其死): Confucius had the same worry about the hard and unbending Zilu.

197.note: "Teaching without words" (不言之教) is teaching by example. Confucius says that if you yourself are upright, things get done without orders.

198.note: "Teaching without words" (不言之教): Confucius too says Heaven does not speak, yet the four seasons run their course.

199.note: Laozi asks "Fame or your person, which is dearer?" (名与身孰亲). Confucius, by contrast, dreads dying without a good name. Here Confucians and Daoists clash head-on over "name."

200.note: "Great eloquence seems tongue-tied" (大辩若讷): Confucius too says those slow of speech are close to ren.

201.note: "Great fullness seems empty" (大盈若冲): Master Zeng says his friend (Yan Yuan, per Zhu Xi) had yet seemed to have nothing, and was full yet seemed empty.

202.note: "No calamity is greater than not knowing contentment" (祸莫大于不知足): Confucius says a state should fear unequal distribution more than scarcity.

203.note: Laozi says "Without going out the door, one knows the world" (不出户，知天下). Confucius says thinking without learning is of no use.

204.note: Su Zhe explains "In pursuing learning, one gains daily" (为学日益) by citing Confucius's "hear much, choose the good and follow it," and calls this only "the next level of knowing."

205.note: Su Zhe goes on to cite Confucius asking Zigong: "I am not one who learns much and remembers it. I have one thread running through it all." This, Su says, is exactly "in pursuing the Dao, one loses daily" (为道日损).

206.note: "Those who are not good, I also treat with goodness" (不善者吾亦善之). Confucius instead advocates "repay resentment with uprightness."

207.note: This chapter of Laozi is entirely about life and death. Confucius says: not yet understanding life, how can one understand death?

208.note: "Produces but does not possess, acts but does not presume" (生而不有，为而不恃): possessing the world without treating it as one's own.

209.note: "Block the openings, shut the doors" (塞其兑，闭其门): Laozi shuts the gates of eyes and ears, while Confucius teaches not to look at or listen to what is contrary to ritual.

210.note: Wang Bi explains "having wealth and goods in excess" (财货有余) with Confucius's words "if not obtained by the proper way."

211.note: "The people love byways" (民好径), while Confucius's school praised Tantai Mieming for "never taking shortcuts": the same little path.

212.note: "Cultivate it in the person, and its virtue will be genuine" (修之于身，其德乃真), extending step by step to the whole world. Confucius says "cultivate oneself to bring peace to the people."

213.note: Heshang Gong explains "Those who speak do not know" (言者不知) with Zigong's saying "a team of four horses cannot overtake the tongue."

214.note: "Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know" (知者不言，言者不知). Confucius says the virtuous will surely have something to say, but those who have something to say are not necessarily virtuous.

215.note: Heshang Gong says "value deeds, not words" (贵行不贵言). Confucius says the gentleman is slow in speech and quick in action.

216.note: Jiao Hong records Xizhai's commentary, which cites "when the wind passes over the grass, it must bend" to explain "I do nothing, and the people transform of themselves" (我无为而民自化).

217.note: Su Zhe explains "The more laws and orders are displayed" (法令滋彰) by citing Confucius's passage on rectifying names: "the people will not know where to put hand or foot."

218.note: "I do nothing, and the people transform of themselves" (我无为而民自化). Confucius too praises Shun for "governing by non-action."

219.note: "Straight but not overbearing" (直而不肆): straightness needs measure. Confucius says straightness without ritual wounds others.

220.note: "Sharp-edged but not cutting" (廉而不刿): Confucius was "gentle yet stern, awe-inspiring yet not fierce." It is the same "A yet not B" pattern.

221.note: "For governing people and serving Heaven, nothing is better than frugality" (治人事天莫若啬): Confucius's governance also stresses "economy in expenditure and love for the people."

222.note: "Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish" (治大国若烹小鲜): commentators explain it through Shun's non-action, and Confucius praises Shun in the same way.

223.note: "When the Dao oversees the world, ghosts lose their spirit-power" (以道莅天下，其鬼不神). Confucius says to respect ghosts and spirits but keep them at a distance.

224.note: "A great state is like the lower reaches of a river" (大国者下流): Zigong says the gentleman most dreads dwelling in the low place, yet Laozi wants the great state to accept the low place willingly.

225.note: "If a great state lowers itself to a small state, it wins the small state" (大国以下小国，则取小国). Confucius says that if distant people do not submit, one should cultivate civil virtue to draw them in.

226.note: Su Zhe explains "Why abandon those who are not good?" (人之不善，何弃之有) with "one who does wrong in the morning yet hears the great Dao in the evening," adapting Confucius's "hear the Way in the morning."

227.note: "Why abandon those who are not good?" (人之不善，何弃之有): Confucius too says that in teaching he made no distinction of background.

228.note: In the Analects, someone puts "repay resentment with virtue" (报怨以德) to Confucius, who answers "repay resentment with uprightness." Zhu Xi notes: "What this person cites…"

229.note: Lü Huiqing explains "Light promises surely lack trust" (轻诺必寡信) through "words that can be made good" (复言). The phrase comes from Master You: "When trust is close to righteousness, one's word can be made good."

230.note: "A nine-story terrace rises from a heap of earth" (九层之台，起于累土): Confucius says that if you stop when the mound is one basketful short, it is you who stopped.

231.note: "Not to enlighten the people but to keep them simple" (非以明民，将以愚之): the two lines are often compared, and both depend on how the old commentaries read them.

232.note: Wang Bi says that if you govern a state by cleverness, the people respond with cleverness. Confucius says that if you govern the people by punishments, they will avoid them but have no sense of shame.

233.note: "To be ahead of the people, one must put oneself behind them" (欲先民，必以身后之): Confucius says that in governing, you yourself should lead the way and take on the toil first.

234.note: "Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him" (以其不争，故天下莫能与之争).

235.note: Jiao Hong records Wang Pang's commentary, which uses Confucius's "In ritual, frugality is better than extravagance" to explain "the second is frugality" (二曰俭).

236.note: "Compassionate, hence able to be brave" (慈故能勇): Confucius too says the humane are surely brave.

237.note: "Frugal, hence able to be generous" (俭故能广). Confucius says "economy in expenditure and love for the people."

238.note: "The good warrior is not martial" (善为士者不武): war was among the matters Confucius treated with the greatest caution.

239.note: "No calamity is greater than underestimating the enemy" (祸莫大于轻敌): what Confucius wanted was someone who "approaches affairs with fear."

240.note: "Military strategists have a saying" (用兵有言), yet Confucius said he had never studied military matters.

241.note: "Wearing coarse cloth while holding jade in the bosom" (被褐怀玉): it is the same jade, but Confucius would "sell it!" while Laozi keeps it tucked away.

242.note: "Those who understand me are few" (知我者希). Confucius too sighed, "No one understands me!"

243.note: "Those who understand me are few; those who follow me are rare" (知我者希，则我者贵). Confucius says not to resent it when others do not understand you.

244.note: "To know that one does not know is highest" (知不知，上): the line where the two schools come closest.

245.note: Confucius calls himself ignorant, which fits neatly with Laozi's "knowing that one does not know."

246.note: "When the people do not fear authority, a greater terror arrives" (民不畏威，则大威至). Confucius speaks of the three things the gentleman holds in awe.

247.note: Su Zhe explains "The way of Heaven does not contend yet excels at winning, does not speak yet excels at responding" by citing Confucius's "What does Heaven ever say?"

248.note: "Bravery in daring means death" (勇于敢则杀): this is exactly what Confucius feared for Zilu.

249.note: "Bravery in not daring means life" (勇于不敢则活): Confucius wanted nothing to do with someone who would fight a tiger bare-handed or wade across a river.

250.note: Su Zhe explains "The people do not fear death" (民不畏死), again citing Confucius: "the people will not know where to put hand or foot."

251.note: "There is always the executioner who does the killing" (常有司杀者杀). Confucius asks why governing should need killing at all.

252.note: Confucius says that if good people governed a state for a hundred years, they could overcome cruelty and do away with killing.

253.note: "The people starve because their rulers tax them too heavily" (民之饥，以其上食税之多). Master You urges Duke Ai to lower taxes: "If the people have enough, with whom will the ruler lack?"

254.note: "The people are hard to govern because those above meddle" (民之难治，以其上之有为). Confucius says that if those above are upright, those below will not dare to be otherwise.

255.note: "The strong and great stay below, the soft and weak stay above" (强大处下，柔弱处上): Master Zeng says his friend (Yan Yuan, per Zhu Xi) had yet seemed to have nothing, and was full yet seemed empty.

256.note: "The way of Heaven reduces surplus and makes up deficiency" (天之道，损有余而补不足). Confucius says the worry is not scarcity but inequality.

257.note: "Who can take his surplus to serve the world?" (孰能有余以奉天下): Confucius says the gentleman helps those in urgent need and does not add to the wealth of the rich.

258.note: Lü Huiqing explains "One who takes on the state's disgrace is called lord of the altars" (受国之垢，是谓社稷主) by citing Tang's words: "If the myriad regions have sinned, the sin rests on my own person"…

259.note: "Taking on the state's misfortunes" (受国不祥): blame yourself much and others little.

260.note: "Reconcile a great resentment, and some resentment surely remains" (和大怨，必有余怨). Confucius advocates "repay resentment with uprightness, and virtue with virtue."

261.note: "The virtuous hold the tally; the virtueless hold the che" (有德司契，无德司彻): che was the Zhou tax system, and Master You urged Duke Ai to adopt it.

262.note: Jiao Hong records Wang Pang's commentary: the Analects and the Mencius both close by invoking Yao, Shun, Yu and Tang, and Laozi ends with this chapter for the same purpose.

263.note: "Neighboring states within sight of one another… the people reach old age and death without ever visiting each other." Confucius, by contrast, wants those near to be glad and those afar to come.

264.note: "Trustworthy words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not trustworthy" (信言不美，美言不信). Confucius says: "Clever words and an ingratiating face: seldom is there ren in them."

265.note: "The good do not argue" (善者不辩). Confucius says the gentleman is slow in speech and quick in action.

266.note: "Those who know are not broadly learned; the broadly learned do not know" (知者不博，博者不知). Confucius teaches broad learning restrained by ritual.
